body: INAAM AMEEN MINHAS, J:- This common judgment shall decide the aforetitled writ petitions, as they involve similar questions of law and facts.

2. In the first two (02) afore-titled writ petitions i.e. W.P. No.’s 989 and 967 of 2025, the petitioners have impugned the amendment made vide SRO. 255(I)/2025 dated 05.03.2025 (“Reconsideration Amendment”), whereby the Civil Servants (Promotion to the post of Secretary, BS-22 and Equivalent) Rules, 2010 (“Rules of 2010”), were amended to the effect that an officer, who had been considered twice for promotion to BS-22 and was not recommended for promotion, was rendered ineligible for further consideration and the petitioners also seek a declaration that the recommendations of the High Powered Selection Board (“HPSB”) which conducted its 29 th Meeting held on 05-10.03.2025 be set aside. The petitioners also seek a direction for consideration to BS-22 with effect from the date when their junior officers were promoted with all consequential benefits.

W.P. NO’S. 989, 967, 1144, 2522, 1085, 1848 AND 1160 OF 2025 3 3. In the writ petitions listed at serial number 3-7, the petitioners in addition to the afore referred prayers have also impugned the notification made vide S.R.O. 35(I)/2025 dated 21.01.2025 (“Impugned Notification”), whereby Bilawal Bhutto Zardari, MNA and Khawaja Muhammad Asif, Minister for Defense were co-opted as members of HPSB, as illegal being ultra vires the Rules of 2010, and the amendment made vide S.R.O. 243(I)/2025 dated 27.02.2025 (“the Chairman Amendment”), whereby the requirement of the Prime Minister chairing HPSB was dispensed with, as illegal having been made without the approval of the Federal Government. The petitioners also seek a declaration that the HPSB was not constituted in accordance with the law and consequently the decisions taken therein are of no legal effect.

4. Apart from the afore stated reliefs sought, in W.P. No. 1160 of 2025 the petitioner has also impugned the amendment made vide S.R.O. (I)/2017 dated 17.07.2017 (“2017 Amendment”) whereby the preamble of the Rules of 2010 and Rule 5 were amended. The petitioner also seeks that his posting as an officer on special duty (“OSD”) made vide notification dated 13.02.2023 (“OSD Notification”) be declared unlawful and the very act of continuing as OSD unlawful. Additionally, the petitioners in W.P. No. 1160 of 2025 and W.P. No. 2522 of 2025 seek a direction for the constitution of the HPSB in terms of the Rules of 2010 as framed originally and to consider afresh the cases of petitioners for promotion to BS-22.

5. Lastly, the petitioner in W.P. No. 2522/2025 has also sought a direction to the respondent to file the exact reasons for non-promotion of the petitioner along with the complete record that was placed before the HPSB for considering the petitioners case for promotion.

A. FACTUAL BACKGROUND 6. The facts leading to the filing of these petitions are that the Prime Minister of Pakistan in his capacity as Chairman of the HPSB invited two persons vide the Impugned Notification namely Bilal Bhutto Zardari, MNA and Khawaja Muhammad Asif, Minister for Defense to attend the 29 th meeting of the HPSB in pursuance of Rule 5 of Rules of 2010. Thereafter, vide the Chairman Amendment the Prime Minister amended the Rules of 2010, and the requirement regarding Prime Minister chairing the HPSB was dispensed with and the entry W.P. NO’S. 989, 967, 1144, 2522, 1085, 1848 AND 1160 OF 2025 4 (a) of rule 5(1) was amended, which now reads as “(a) Prime Minister or a Federal Minister authorized by him in his behalf as Chairman.” Thereafter, on 10.03.2025, a Press Release was issued by the Establishment Division, stating the results of the 29 th Meeting of HPSB. This Press Release showed that multiple juniors to the petitioners were promoted instead of the petitioners. The petitioners in all these petitions are civil servants presently serving in BS-21 and were eligible to be considered for promotion to BS-22 by the HPSB. The Board, after deliberation in its 29 th meeting decided not to recommend the petitioners for promotion and consequently their cases were sent to the competent authority, i.e. the Prime Minister, for consideration of the recommendations who accorded his approval and consequently the recommendations of the HPSB stood affirmed. From the Press Release it also transpired that the meeting was presided over by Muhammad Ishaq Dar the Deputy Prime Minister.

B. ARGUMENTS OF THE PARTIES I. SUBMISSIONS OF THE PETITIONERS 7. The learned counsels appearing on behalf of the petitioners advanced the following submissions, which are reproduced in consolidated form for the sake of convenience:i) The first argument advanced by the learned counsels was that the Impugned Amendments are ultra vires the Civil Servants Act, 1973 (“the Act”) and the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973 (“Constitution”). They contended that according to the well-settled canon of delegated legislation, a piece of subordinate legislation may only be amended by the same authority that enacted it. In this regard they submitted that the Rules of 2010 were framed by the Federal Government in exercise of powers delegated by the President under Section 25(1) of the Act. Since the Rules of 2010 were promulgated by the Federal Government and not by the Prime Minister in his individual capacity, the Impugned Amendments issued by the Prime Minister alone are ultra vires the parent statute and the Cconstitution. Reliance was placed on the case of Mustafa Impex v. Government of Pakistan, (PLD 2016 SC 808) in which the Honorable Supreme Court authoritatively held that the Federal Government comprises the Prime Minister and the Federal Cabinet W.P. NO’S. 989, 967, 1144, 2522, 1085, 1848 AND 1160 OF 2025 5 collectively. The Prime Minister is the head of the Cabinet but is not, in himself, a surrogate or substitute for the Federal Government. He cannot unilaterally exercise powers that are vested in the Cabinet as a whole. Thus, the Impugned Amendments, having been made by the Prime Minister without Cabinet sanction, are void ab initio for want of competence.

ii) With regards to the Chairman Amendment notified on 27.02.2025, which substituted Rule 5(1)(a) of the Rules of 2010 to provide that the HPSB may be chaired by the Prime Minister or a Federal Minister authorized by him in that behalf, the learned counsels contended that the President delegated rule-making authority to the Federal Government under Section 25 of the Act. That authority was not, and could not be, further sub-delegated by the Prime Minister in his individual capacity. The Impugned Amendments are accordingly a nullity in the eyes of law and this principle delegatus non potest delegare operates with full force in the present context which states that an authority to which a power has been delegated cannot further delegate that power.

iii) The learned counsels regarding the Reconsideration Amendment notified on 05.03.2025, submitted that the amendment provides that an officer who has been deferred or not recommended on two occasions by the HPSB shall be rendered permanently ineligible for further consideration for promotion to BPS-22 which is irrational and violative of the petitioner’s fundamental rights. The learned counsels submitted that this amendment is arbitrary, unreasonable, and irrational on its face, and offends Articles 4, 9, 10-A, 12, 25, and 27 of the Constitution. They argued that a civil servant may be deferred by the HPSB for a variety of reasons entirely unrelated to his or her merit, fitness, or suitability for promotion. These include incompleteness of the service record, the officer's absence on ex-Pakistan leave, and pendency of disciplinary or criminal proceedings not yet resulting in conviction, the officer being on deputation or training, or the temporary unavailability of posts. The Reconsideration Amendment, in sweeping and indiscriminate terms, treats all deferrals as equivalent to a finding of unsuitability, and permanently bars the officer from future consideration. It was contended W.P. NO’S. 989, 967, 1144, 2522, 1085, 1848 AND 1160 OF 2025 6 that this conflation of procedurally motivated deferrals with merit-based rejections is logically indefensible and constitutionally impermissible. iv) Furthermore, the learned counsels argued that by imposing a permanent disqualification in consequence of two prior considerations, even where no finding of unfitness was ever communicated to the officer, the Reconsideration Amendment operates as the functional equivalent of a major penalty under the Government Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules, 1973. It is settled law that no major penalty may be imposed upon a civil servant without affording him a notice of the allegations against him and a reasonable opportunity of being heard. They submitted that the Reconsideration Amendment imposes precisely such a penalty, the permanent termination of promotional prospects without any process whatsoever. This constitutes a violation of Article 10-A of the Constitution, which guarantees the right to a fair trial and due process. v) Learned counsels further argued that the retrospective application of the Reconsideration Amendment is constitutionally prohibited. They argued that the Impugned Amendments have been applied retrospectively to the petitioners, in that the working papers for the consideration of the petitioners’ cases had been prepared and finalized in the week preceding 05.03.2025, and the eligibility of the petitioners had been fully established under the Rules of 2010 as they then stood. They submitted that the Reconsideration Amendment was notified on 05.03.2025, the very day of the HPSB meeting, and were applied to exclude the petitioners from consideration despite their pre-existing eligibility. Moreover, they submitted that the retrospective operation of such legislation is expressly prohibited by Article 12 of the Constitution, and the Honorable Supreme Court has consistently struck down such measures.

vi) The next argument advanced was that the 29 th meeting of HPSB was coram non judice since the HPSB was not constituted in accordance with the law and the Impugned Decisions are void ab initio. In this regard they submitted that the Rules of 2010, as originally promulgated, provide unambiguously that the Prime Minister of Pakistan shall be the Chairman of the HPSB. The SRO No. 243(I)/2025 purportedly amended this W.P. NO’S. 989, 967, 1144, 2522, 1085, 1848 AND 1160 OF 2025 7 provision to allow the Prime Minister to authorize “a Federal Minister” to chair the Board in his place. However, even accepting the validity of this amendment arguendo, the 29 th meeting was presided over not by a Federal Minister but by the Deputy Prime Minister, Muhammad Ishaq Dar. Learned counsels submitted that the office/post of “Deputy Prime Minister” is not a constitutionally recognized post under the Constitution, and the Deputy Prime Minister does not hold the office of “Prime Minister” nor has he been shown to have received any lawful authorization from the Prime Minister to preside over the HPSB in compliance with the amended rules. The meetings were accordingly presided over by a person who had no legal authority to do so, rendering all proceedings and recommendations void ab initio and coram non judice. vii) Learned counsels further submitted that participation of unauthorized persons vitiated the proceedings. In this regard they submitted that Rule 5 of the Rules of 2010, as originally framed, permits the Chairman of the HPSB to invite officers holding posts in BPS-22 for consultation where deemed appropriate. The 2017 amendment to the said rule expanded this provision marginally to allow the Chairman to additionally invite Federal Ministers, Ministers of State, Advisors, and Special Assistants to the Prime Minister. Notwithstanding these provisions, the meetings of the HPSB of 05.03.2025 and 10.03.2025 were attended by Bilawal Bhutto Zardari, who at the material time held the office of Member of the National Assembly and not any of the offices specified in Rule 5. His presence in the deliberations of the HPSB was entirely without legal authority and in flagrant violation of the Rules of 2010. The participation of an intruder in proceedings of a statutory body is sufficient, in itself, to vitiate the entire proceedings and render the recommendations of such body a nullity. In addition, the Impugned Notification of 21.01.2025 inviting Bilawal Bhutto Zardari and Khawaja Muhammad Asif to attend the upcoming HPSB meeting was issued by the Prime Minister in purported exercise of the Chairman's power under Rule 5. However, the Prime Minister did not chair the actual meeting of 05.03.2025. Since the power under Rule 5 to invite additional participants is personal to the Chairman, and since the Chairman of the 05.03.2025 meeting was, in fact, W.P. NO’S. 989, 967, 1144, 2522, 1085, 1848 AND 1160 OF 2025 8 the Deputy Prime Minister, the invitations issued by the Prime Minister on 21.01.2025 had no legal efficacy for purposes of that meeting. They further submitted that the Impugned Notification through which elected politicians were invited not only politicizes the HPSB, but the same does not qualify under Rule 5 since the invited members are not officers in BPS-22 and unauthorized to participate in deliberations on the fitness and suitability of civil servants for promotion. The Rules of 2010 were framed expressly to insulate senior bureaucratic appointments from political interference, in the spirit of the Supreme Court’s ruling in the Tariq Azizud-Din case reported as 2010 SCMR 1301. Thus, they submitted that the th meeting of HPSB was void ab initio and coram non judice.

viii) The next argument advanced by the learned counsels was that the HPSB violated the principles of natural justice. The learned counsels argued that the HPSB was bound to act within the four corners of the law but their actions exhibit a capricious and unfettered exercise of discretion. Reliance was placed on the case of Tariq Aziz-ud-Din (ibid), wherein the Court held that civil servants, while they do not possess an absolute right to promotion, are vested with an indefeasible right to be fairly and lawfully considered for promotion. Learned counsels submitted that withholding of promotion from a civil servant who is otherwise eligible and senior constitutes a major penalty within the meaning of the Government Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules, 1973, and cannot lawfully be imposed upon such a civil servant except in accordance with due process of law, upon the basis of tangible material, and after affording the concerned officer an opportunity to be heard. However, in the cases at hand, no reasons have ever been communicated, no adverse material was placed before the petitioners, and no opportunity to rebut any such material was afforded to them. The non-recommendation of the petitioners in favor of their juniors has been affected without a shred of recorded reasoning capable of withstanding scrutiny. They argued that the Courts have consistently and emphatically deprecated the noncommunication of reasons for deferment or supersession as being violative of Articles 4 and 10-A of the Constitution and of Section 24-A of the General Clauses Act, 1897, which mandates that every authority W.P. NO’S. 989, 967, 1144, 2522, 1085, 1848 AND 1160 OF 2025 9 exercising statutory power shall do so reasonably, fairly, and justly, and shall record reasons for its decisions. The impugned recommendations of the HPSB are thus arbitrary, in excess of jurisdiction, and liable to be set aside.

ix) Lastly, the learned counsels submitted that the circumstances surrounding the issuance of the Impugned Amendments and the proceedings of the HPSB meeting is tainted with mala fide. In particular, the attention of this Court is drawn to the following; the amendment of 05.03.2025 was notified on the very day that the HPSB met, apparently in reaction to the orders of this Court in writ proceedings then pending; the working papers for the petitioners consideration had been completed in the preceding week, demonstrating their eligibility under the thenprevailing rules; and the amendment was applied on the very day of its notification, with the admitted purpose of excluding the petitioners from consideration. These facts, taken together, compel the inference that the Impugned Amendments were designed to circumvent judicial scrutiny and to favor particular blue eyed officers by engineering the disqualification of the petitioners and the deliberate circumvention of these safeguards vitiates the entire exercise.

II. ARGUMENTS OF THE RESPONDENTS 8. Conversely, the learned Additional Attorney General raised preliminary objection to the maintainability of the writ petitions by contending that the petitioners are civil servants whose terms and conditions of service are governed exclusively by the Act, and the bar contained in Article 212 of the Constitution is squarely attracted, therefore, matters relating to the terms and conditions of service, including promotion and determination of suitability, fall within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Federal Service Tribunal (“FST”). He submitted that u/s 23-B of the Act only FST has jurisdiction to hear the cases of the civil servants. It was further contended that the minutes of meeting of the HPSB which contains its assessment and collective judgment have been declared confidential in nature by the Minister-in-Charge and in the absence of any explicit rule in the Rules of 2010, the same are not liable to be disclosed. The learned Additional Attorney General without prejudice to the afore-stated W.P. NO’S. 989, 967, 1144, 2522, 1085, 1848 AND 1160 OF 2025 10 objection, contended on merits that the evaluation of the petitioners was undertaken within a regulated framework of structured discretion prescribed by the Rules of 2010 as mandated by the decision of the Honorable Supreme Court of Pakistan in Federation of Pakistan vs. Dr. Muhammad Arif & Others, (2017 SCMR 969). He further contended that the HPSB acted strictly in accordance with law without discrimination or mala fide and decisions regarding promotions rest firmly within the domain of the competent executive authorities whose professional expertise, institutional knowledge, and familiarity with the functional requirements of senior civil service positions ensure fairness, impartiality, and integrity in the process.

9. I have given anxious consideration to the arguments of the learned counsel for the parties and perused the record with their able assistance. C. OBJECTIONS I. MAINTAINABILITY 10. Before entering upon the merits of the matter, it is necessary to first address the objection as to the maintainability raised by the learned Additional Attorney General who contended that this Court’s jurisdiction was ousted by Article 212 of the Constitution in matters relating to the terms and conditions of service of the civil servants and that the matter falls within the exclusive jurisdiction of the FST which is competent to decide the matter even in the presence of challenge to the vires of Impugned Amendments. However, the same is misconceived since for this contention to hold merit, the matter must fall within the jurisdiction of FST. Only if this threshold is met would the second question arise i.e. whether the FST is competent to decide the questions of vires. It is settled position that the FST is competent to examine questions of vires incidental to matters falling within its jurisdiction but that competence cannot be invoked to manufacture jurisdiction over a matter that falls outside the FST’s statutory jurisdiction.

Iqan Ahmed Khurram vs. Government, (PLD 1980 SC 153), Muhammad Hashim Khan vs. Province of Balochistan, (PLD 1976 Quetta 59), Muhammad Hashim Khan vs. Province of Balochistan, (PLD 1976 Quetta 59), Muhammad Anis vs. Abdul Haseeb, (PLD 1994 SC 539) and I.A. Sherwani and others vs. Government of Pakistan through Secretary Finance Division, Islamabad and others, (1991 SCMR 1041).

W.P. NO’S. 989, 967, 1144, 2522, 1085, 1848 AND 1160 OF 2025 11 11. At this juncture it is appropriate to state that apart from the challenge to vires these cases pertain to promotion of the petitioners to posts in BS-22 and essentially relates to the determination of their fitness for the posts in question. It is settled law that assessment of fitness and suitability are excluded from the jurisdiction of the FST under section 4 of the Federal Service Tribunals Act, 1973. The position has been best explained by the Honorable Supreme Court in the case of Aftab Ahmed Maneka in the following manner:- “13. We first attend to the preliminary objections raised on behalf of learned Attorney-General to the maintainability of the Writ Petitions filed before the High Court on the touchstone of Article 212 of the Constitution. Article 212(1)(a) is an enabling provisions empowering the legislature to establish Tribunals exercising exclusive jurisdiction in matters relating to the terms and conditions of service of persons who are or have been in the Service of Pakistan. It is in view of this Constitutional provision that the Federal Service Tribunal Act, 1973 was enacted. Clause (2) of Article 212 of the Constitution excludes the jurisdiction of all Courts in matters falling within the exclusive jurisdiction of Tribunal set up under Clause (1) of Article 212 of the Constitution. It reads:

"(2) Notwithstanding anything hereinbefore contained where any Administrative Court or Tribunal is established under clause (1), no other court shall grant an injunction, make any order or entertain any proceedings in respect of any matter to which the jurisdiction of such Administrative Court or Tribunal extends and all proceedings in respect of any such matter which may be pending before such other court immediately before the establishment of the Administrative Court or Tribunal; other than an appeal pending before the Supreme Court, shall abate on such establishment." [Emphasis is ours] Section 4 of the Federal Service Tribunal Act, 1973 provides for appeals to the Tribunal by a civil servant aggrieved of any order regarding terms and conditions of his service. Clause (b) of subsection (1) of section 4 of the Federal Service Tribunal Act expressly bars the Tribunal from entertaining appeal against the decision of a departmental Authority determining the fitness or other wise of a person to be promoted to a higher grade. The Tribunal has thus no jurisdiction to examine whether or not a civil servant is fit for promotion to a higher grade. Under Clause (2) of Article 212 of the Constitution the jurisdiction of the Court is ousted only over matters falling within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Tribunal established under Clause (1) of Article 212. As the determination of fitness of a civil servant for promotion has been Secretary Establishment Division vs. Aftab Ahmed Maneka, (2015 SCMR 1006). W.P. NO’S. 989, 967, 1144, 2522, 1085, 1848 AND 1160 OF 2025 12 excluded from jurisdiction of the Tribunal, the ouster Clause (2) of Article 212 therefore does not extend to such matters.”

From the perusal of above it is evident that the jurisdiction of High Court is not barred, where the issue pertains to fitness for promotion. As a consequence, the bar contained under Article 212 is not attracted to the present cases and the same has been categorically held by the superior courts in numerous cases. II. CONFIDENTIALITY 12. The second objection was raised when this Court, in order to ascertain the veracity of the claims regarding arbitrariness and unfair consideration for promotion, directed that the minutes of the meeting of HPSB and the complete record placed before the HPSB be placed before this Court. At this juncture, the learned Additional Attorney General raised the objection of confidentiality and reliance was placed upon section 7(f) of the Right of Access to Information Act, 2017. For ease the relevant portion is reproduced below:- “7. Exclusion of certain record. —Nothing contained in section 6 shall apply to the following record of all public bodies, namely: — (a)… (b)… (c)… (d)… (e)… (f) record declared as classified by the Minister-in-charge of the Federal Government:

Provided that the Minister-in-charge of the Federal Government shall have to record reasons as to why the harm from disclosure of information outweighs public interest and further that information pertaining to allegation of corruption and violation of human rights shall not be excluded.”

13. A bare perusal of section 7(f) unambiguously reveals that the exclusion from disclosure is neither automatic nor unconditional. The provision contemplates a two-fold statutory requirement before any record can be lawfully withheld on the ground of confidentiality. Firstly, the record must have been Orya Maqbool Jan vs. Federation of Pakistan through Secretary and others, (2014 SCMR 817), I.A. Sherwani and others vs. Government of Pakistan through Secretary Finance Division, Islamabad and others, (1991 SCMR 1041), Mian Abdul Malik vs. Dr. Sabir Zameer Siddiqui and 4 others, (1991 SCMR 1129).

W.P. NO’S. 989, 967, 1144, 2522, 1085, 1848 AND 1160 OF 2025 13 expressly declared as “classified” by the Minister-in-charge of the Federal Government. Secondly, even such declaration is subject to a mandatory obligation upon the Minister-in-charge to record reasons demonstrating that the harm likely to result from disclosure outweighs the public interest involved. The proviso further circumscribes the scope of exclusion by expressly providing that information pertaining to allegations of corruption or violation of human rights shall not fall within the exclusionary ambit. In the present matter, the first requirement is satisfied since the record has been declared as classified by the Prime Minister who at that time was the minister in Charge. However, the respondents have failed to satisfy the second statutory requirement of section 7(f) which stipulates that the Minister in Charge shall record reasons demonstrating that the harm likely to result from disclosure outweighs the public interest involved. The Prime Minister/Minister in Charge’s approval dated 10.01.2022 reflects that no reasons were recorded to justify the classification of such record as “classified”. Equally absent is the recording of reasons to establish that the harm from disclosure outweighs the overriding public interest. It is settled law that statutory power cannot be exercised in an unstructured, unguided, or unbridled manner, for such exercise undermines the statutory scheme . It would be more appropriate to examine the matter through the lens of the standard in which the Minister in Charge, must invariably ask himself: what order should I pass if I were to act justly, fairly, and reasonably? If the order ultimately passed is inconsistent with the answer to that question, he would exceed his lawful jurisdiction. Reasonableness in this context requires a demonstrable application of mind, a conscious evaluation of the circumstances warranting the exclusion of the record from “Public Record”, and the articulation of reasons that reveal a rational nexus between the standard that the harm from disclosure outweighs the overriding public interest. However, it is evident from the record that the Minister in Charge mechanically categorized the record as “classified” and did not address the statutory preconditions. In the absence of Walayat Ali Mir vs. Pakistan International Airlines Corporation, (1995 SCMR 650), Aman Ullah Khan and others vs. The Federal Government of Pakistan through Secretary, Ministry of Finance, Islamabad and others, (PLD 1990 SC 1092), Chairman Regional Transport Authority, Rawalpindi vs. Pakistan Mutual Insurance Company Limited, Rawalpindi, (PLD 1991 SC 14), Government of N.W.F.P. through Secretary and 3 others vs. Mejee Flour and General Mills (Pvt.) Ltd. Mardan and others, (1997 SCMR 1804), Abid Hussain and others vs. P.I.A.C. and others, (2005 SCMR 25), Messrs Gadoon Textile Mills and 814 others vs. WAPDA and others, (1997 SCMR 641), Abu Bakar Siddique and others vs. Collector of Customs, Lahore and others, (2006 SCMR 705) W.P. NO’S. 989, 967, 1144, 2522, 1085, 1848 AND 1160 OF 2025 14 compliance with these statutory pre-conditions, the plea of confidentiality remains a mere assertion devoid of legal backing. The contention of the respondents that the record is confidential, without fulfilling the mandatory statutory requirements enshrined in section 7(f) of the Right of Access to Information Act, 2017 cannot be sustained.

14. Even otherwise, the reliance upon section 7(f) is misconceived inasmuch as the minutes of meeting forms the very basis of the Impugned Decisions affecting the petitioners’ promotion prospects. Denial of access to such material, while simultaneously relying upon it to the detriment of the petitioners, offends the principles of transparency, fairness, and due process, and renders the decision-making process opaque and arbitrary. The same, therefore, amounts to nothing more than a bare assertion of confidentiality, which carries no legal sanctity and is liable to be disregarded in proceedings of judicial review. Moreover, this Court has already addressed the contention of confidentiality in the case of Babar Bashir , in the following manner:- “13. This Court would like to take exception to the plea that the objective assessment and marks awarded by the DSB are “confidential” and therefore immune from disclosure. Quite frankly this cannot be accepted as an absolute proposition of law. While it is settled that promotion to a selection post is not a vested right and that the assessment of fitness lies primarily within the domain of the competent authority, such discretion is neither unfettered nor insulated from judicial scrutiny. Confidentiality cannot be invoked as a cloak to defeat the requirements of fairness, transparency, and due process, particularly where it results in an adverse outcome such as supersession of a civil servant. The right asserted by the petitioner is not to promotion per se, but to a fair, reasoned, and lawful consideration in accordance with the governing rules. Where the decision results in supersession, the minimum requirement of law is that the affected officer be made aware of the basis of the decision, at least to the extent necessary to enable him to understand why he failed to meet the prescribed threshold and to meaningfully assail the decision if it is arbitrary or perverse… Judicial precedent has consistently held that while courts do not sit as appellate forums over the wisdom of Selection Boards, they are competent to examine whether the process adopted was lawful, transparent, and free from arbitrariness or mala fides. Non-disclosure of marks or reasons, especially when allegations of “average competence” and “questionable integrity” are levelled without prior communication or supporting material, renders the process doubtful and offends the principles of natural justice. Confidentiality, therefore, cannot be stretched to justify Writ Petition No. 3715 of 2024 titled “Babar Bashir vs. Federation of Pakistan and others”. W.P. NO’S. 989, 967, 1144, 2522, 1085, 1848 AND 1160 OF 2025 15 non-communication of reasons or to shield an otherwise reviewable decision from judicial review, particularly where the action complained of is supersession and that too which frustrates the legitimate expectation of fair consideration under the law.”

15. The above referred case related to the Babar Bashir’s consideration for promotion by the Department Selection Board, however, the same observation applies with equal force in these matters and the plea of confidentiality, as raised by the respondents, cannot be accepted as an absolute bar to disclosure before this Court, particularly where the impugned decisions are alleged to be procedurally improper, irrational, arbitrary and tainted with mala fide. D. QUESTIONS FOR DETERMINATION 16. Tersely recapitulated, the petitioners in all the writ petitions are civil servants and were eligible to be considered for promotion in BS-22 by the HPSB in its 29 th meeting, however, they were not recommended for promotion vide the Impugned Decisions. While considering the background of the petitions, the grounds raised by the parties and question of law involved, the following questions need adjudication by this Court:i) Whether the Impugned Amendments are unconstitutional and ultra vires the Civil Servants Act, 1973 and the Constitution of 1973?

ii) Whether the 29 th meeting of the HPSB was lawfully constituted and conducted in accordance with the Rules of 2010? iii) Whether the Impugned Decisions of the HPSB are liable to be set aside on the grounds that the Board failed to accord meaningful consideration to the petitioner’s cases for promotion? iv) Whether the OSD Notification, as well as the act of Respondent No. 1 in continuing the petitioner in W.P. No. 1160 of 2025 as an OSD for the past two years, is unlawful?

E. CHALLENGE TO THE VIRES 17. To address the first question framed, it is necessary to briefly examine the relevant statutory framework, and the delegating provision that governs the exercise of the delegated legislative power. The Rules of 2010 were promulgated by the Federal Government in the exercise of powers derived from Section 25(1) of the Act which is the delegating provision in the parent statute and goes to the root of the entire matter. Section 25 of the Act is reproduced below:- W.P. NO’S. 989, 967, 1144, 2522, 1085, 1848 AND 1160 OF 2025 16 “25. Rules.- (1) The President, or any person authorised by the President in this behalf, may make such rules as appear to him to be necessary or expedient for carrying out the purposes of this Act. (2) Any rules, orders or instructions in respect of any terms and conditions of service of civil servants duly made or issued by an authority competent to make them and in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall, in so far as such rules, orders or instructions are not inconsistent with the provisions of this Act, be deemed to be rules made under this Act.”

A plain reading of Section 25(1) reveals two distinct limbs of rule-making authority. First, the power is vested in the President as the principal authority. Second, the President is expressly empowered to delegate this authority to any person he may authorize in that behalf. A bare perusal of Section 25 reflects that the same vests the rule-making power in the President, with an enabling clause permitting delegation to such person or authority as may be authorized by him. It is manifest from the record that by virtue of S.R.O. 120(I)/98, promulgated in 1998 by the President in exercise of the authority conferred by Section 25(1) of the Civil Servants Act, the President expressly authorized the Prime Minister to make rules under the Act. This delegation is of utmost importance since it is specific in its subject matter (rule-making under the Act), express in its conferment (the authorization is unambiguously directed to the Prime Minister), and valid in law (it flows from a constitutional and statutory authority fully competent to delegate). 22. The reliance on the doctrine in Mustafa Impex must, accordingly, be understood in its proper context. The Supreme Court’s holding in that case addresses the distinction between the Prime Minister acting in his personal capacity and the Federal Government acting as a collective constitutional body. It does not address the distinct circumstance where the President has made an express and specific delegation of a statutory power directly to the Prime Minister. When the Prime Minister exercises authority that has been personally conferred upon him by the President under a statutory provision, he does not purport to act as the Federal Government, rather he acts as the authorized delegate of the President. The two situations are legally distinct and must not be conflated. The principle in Mustafa Impex is directed at preventing the Prime Minister from appropriating to himself powers constitutionally or statutorily vested in the Federal Government collectively. It has no application where the Prime Minister exercises power in his own name, by virtue of an express delegation in his name from the constitutionally competent authority. To hold otherwise would be to render the enabling clause in Section 25(1), “or any person authorised by the President” irrelevant, redundant and illusory, which W.P. The Federal Government is a distinct constitutional entity under Article 90 of the Constitution, functioning collectively through the Cabinet. It is neither synonymous with nor interchangeable with the Prime Minister acting individually when authorized. Thus, the reliance on the case of Mustafa Impex is misconceived.

23. Moreover, even if the original promulgation of the Rules of 2010 by the “Federal Government” created an ambiguity as to the identity of the promulgating authority, given that the delegation under S.R.O. 120(I)/98 was in favour of the Prime Minister individually, the 2017 Amendment operates as a curative measure that resolves that ambiguity definitively and prospectively. An authority competent in law when subsequently exercises a power in respect of an earlier instrument, such subsequent exercise operates to cure any procedural or formal defect that may have attended the earlier action. The curative principle does not require the invalidity of the earlier action to be established, it suffices that the subsequent exercise of power, by the competent authority, regularizes and reaffirms the basis upon which the earlier instrument was made. In the present case, the Prime Minister as the lawful and express delegate of the President for rule-making under the Act amended the preamble of the Rules of 2010 which explicitly acknowledged that the rules were being made by him in exercise of his delegated authority. This act of clarification was squarely within the scope of the delegation under S.R.O. 120(I)/98 and necessary after the judgment in Mustafa Impex. Far from being an unauthorized usurpation of power, it was an exercise of existing and valid authority, which had the additional effect of removing any residual uncertainty regarding the identity of the lawful rule-maker.

The need for delegated legislation arises to reduce pressure on parliamentary time and to make provision for rapidly changing or uncertain situations which may or may not be in the contemplation of the Parliament. In essence this is the exercise of an executive function that the rule has created and authorized and is a distinct act which does not pertain to law-making. The maxim delegatus non potest delegare does not prohibit a delegate from arranging the manner in which administrative functions under a rule are to be carried out, unless the parent act requires personal performance of the function. 39. This principle, correctly understood, does not demand the exclusion of the political executive from all contact with the civil service promotion process. On the contrary, it requires that each branch and organ of the State operate within its constitutionally and statutorily assigned domain, without undue encroachment by the judiciary into the domain of the executive. Thus, this Court is disinclined to indulge in such an assessment. The powers delegated to the Authority for framing rules generally signify broad discretion reserved for it to make assessment as to what will advance the purposes of the parent statute and also the measures required to advance those purposes. The rule-making authority in the present matter is vested, by specific statutory delegation, in the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister, acting within that delegated authority, determined that the Chairman of the HPSB should have the discretion to seek consultation from senior members of the political executive. That determination is an exercise of executive judgment within the executive domain. For this Court to invalidate that exercise on the ground that it disagrees with the policy rationale behind it would itself constitute a violation of the doctrine of separation of powers. It is generally recognized that issues which relate to policy matters involve greater expertise and are thus left to be determined by the delegated agencies. Implicit in this deferential attitude is the acknowledgement that the Courts should not engage in policy analysis for various reasons. Since the present controversy stems from not being accorded fair meaningful consideration for promotion which is governed under the Rules of 2010, it is important to take a brief look at the genesis of these rules and appreciate the spirit behind them. The Rules of 2010 owe their genesis directly W.P. NO’S. 989, 967, 1144, 2522, 1085, 1848 AND 1160 OF 2025 35 to the case of Tariq Aziz-ud-Din reported as (2010 SCMR 1301). The petitioner, Tariq Aziz-ud-din was a BPS-21 officer of the Foreign Service Group who had been superseded without merit. Aggrieved, he wrote a letter to the Chief Justice of Pakistan and the matter was converted into a human rights case. The Supreme Court noted that this particular class of promotions i.e. from 21 to 22 were, at the time, not regulated by any specific set of rules. This situation had arisen because the Civil Servants (Appointment and Tenure of Post in BPS-22) Rules, 1993 had been rescinded on 4 th April, 1998. The Supreme Court held that the general legal principle of merit-based promotions equally applies to promotions from BPS 21 to 22 and these are not “discretionary” or political appointments. The Court reaffirmed the principle that denial of promotion is a major penalty, therefore, in order to be sustainable before a court of law, the process of promotions, including the promotions from BPS-21 to BPS-22 must be transparent and competitive. The Court set aside the promotion of 54 officers, while directing the competent authority to consider all cases afresh. The Honorable Supreme Court also observed that, “It would be appreciated that to ensure fairness and justness, the Rules rescinded on 4 th April, 1998 are reenacted accordingly.” It was in pursuance of the Supreme Court’s observations in Tariq Aziz-ud-Did (Supra) that the Federal Government decided to promulgate, on 16 th August, the Rules of 2010. The object and purpose were to ensure that only those who are demonstrably higher in terms of merit will be promoted and furthermore, that the discretion vested in the competent authority for promoting civil servants will not be used for favoring blue-eyed candidates on the basis of political considerations.

The Rules of 2010, however, do not delineate in explicit terms the criteria or weightage governing the exercise of discretion by the HPSB. This position stands in contrast to later regulatory frameworks, such as Civil Servants Promotion (BS-18 to BS-21) Rules, 2019, wherein discretion has been more elaborately structured through defined benchmarks and evaluation parameters. W.P. I. ILLEGALITY 51. This Court shall now examine whether the decision-making process reflects lawful exercise of discretion or suffers from any illegality. The perusal of para 8 of the minutes of the HPSB’s meeting reveals a downright shocking situation of exercise of discretion in an unbridled manner. The Board resolved to evaluate officers not only on the basis of their service record, Performance Evaluation Reports, Training Evaluation Reports, and other documentable criteria, but also on the basis of attributes “as known to the Board members.” This parameter or criteria demands the closest scrutiny since it affords unfettered discretion which is a flagrant illegality. In this regard it necessary to see how the courts have interpreted the limits of discretion. In the case of Montgomery Flour and General Mills Ltd., Montgomery vs. The Director, Food Purchases, West Pakistani (PLD 1957 Lah, 914) the following was observed:- “It should be remembered that no discretion vested in an executive officer is an absolute and arbitrary discretion. The discretion is vested in him for a public purpose and must be exercised for the W.P. NO’S. 989, 967, 1144, 2522, 1085, 1848 AND 1160 OF 2025 42 attainment of that purpose. Even though there be no express words in the relevant legal provision to that effect, the discretion is always circumscribed by the scope and the object of the law that creates it and has at the same time to be exercised justly, fairly and reasonably.”

Similarly in Abid Hasan vs. PIAC, (2005 SCMR 25) the Court observed:- “If the judicial administrative organs of the State while applying the law were to discriminate between man and man and exercise what may be characterized as arbitrary authority in singling out some persons for discriminatory treatment they would be acting counter to the ideal of equality before law which has been proclaimed by the framers of the Constitution in the first part of the clause of Article 5 an Article which declares that all citizens are equal before law. It would thus be noticed that notion of human equality had emerged as a reaction to abhorring artificial 'distinctions between man and man or between one class of men and another class based on consideration, inter alia, of personal likes and. dislikes -under the garb of discretion.

It was laid down in the case of Dr. Muhammad Arif that the consideration of an officer for promotion is to be based not only on the relevant law and rules but also on some tangible material. III. PROCEDURAL IMPROPRIETY 65. Another aspect of fair and meaningful consideration would be whether the consideration is free from procedural impropriety, which operates through two distinct but overlapping mechanisms. First is the failure to observe statutory procedural requirements. The second limb of procedural impropriety is the breach of natural justice. While it is hard to exactly define the boundaries of natural justice, it can be safely said that natural justice embodies the fundamental rights, different rules of fair play, due process and other rights, which may be treated as fundamental, even though not enumerated in the Constitution. Whatever disagreement there may be as to the scope of “natural justice”, there is no doubt that it generally always includes the right to be heard and adherence to the principle of audi alteram partem i.e. no one should be condemned unheard. It is settled law that every person is entitled to have due notice of proceedings, which effects his rights along with being afforded a reasonable opportunity to defend . For its application, the rule does not depend upon whether the proceedings are judicial or quasi-judicial or administrative or quasi Aftab Shahban Mirani vs. President of Pakistan, (1998 SCMR 1863) and New Jubilee Insurance vs. National Bank of Pakistan, (PLD 1999 SC 1126).

67. The second plane of procedural impropriety relates to communication. It transpires that the officers in the present petitions were superseded without being informed of the reasons, the material, or the findings that led the Board to that determination. This non-disclosure strikes at the heart of the principles of natural justice and procedural fairness, as the petitioners have been deprived of knowledge of the grounds of their non-promotion and, consequently, of any meaningful opportunity to question or challenge the assessment. This obligation of communication is not derived solely from the common law of natural justice, though it is firmly grounded there. It finds independent and express constitutional support in three provisions of the Constitution of Pakistan. Article 4 imposes upon every public functionary the obligation to act justly, fairly, and without arbitrariness toward every citizen. An authority that withholds from an officer the grounds of his supersession cannot, by any measure, be said to have acted justly or fairly toward him. Article 10-A, introduced through the Eighteenth Amendment, guarantees the right to a fair trial and due process in the determination of civil rights and obligations, a right that is rendered wholly meaningless if an affected officer is denied knowledge of the case against him. Article 19-A guarantees the right of access to information in all matters of public importance, a right that is directly engaged when an officer is denied access to the findings and material that have determined the course of his career.

68. The Lahore High Court, in Humaira Hassan (Supra), examined the obligations of the HPSB and held that the Board is under a constitutional and legal obligation to communicate its recommendation to the concerned civil servant and not to keep it under wraps to the disadvantage and inconvenience of the civil servant. The Court further condemned this ring of secrecy by stating, “this undesired and unnecessary ring of secrecy leaves the civil servant groping in an abyss of uncertainty, which besides lowering her morale and confidence restricts her right to access to justice.” The same observation applies with equal force to the seven petitioners before this Court, each of whom was left without W.P. The obligation to communicate reasons is further reinforced by section 24-A of the General Clauses Act, 1897, which mandates that every statutory power be exercised reasonably, fairly, justly, and for the advancement of the purposes of the enactment under which it is conferred. The superior Courts have, in a consistent and unbroken line of authority, interpreted this provision to require that executive authorities exercising discretionary powers issue speaking orders i.e. orders that articulate the reasons upon which the decision is founded.

69. This requirement of reasoned decision-making is neither a procedural formality nor an administrative courtesy. It is a substantive safeguard that serves three distinct and essential functions. First, it ensures that the decision-maker has applied its mind genuinely and objectively to the matter before it, rather than acting upon impulse, prejudice, or predetermined conclusion. Second, it apprises the affected person of the basis of the action taken against him, thereby enabling him to exercise whatever rights of appeal, review, or challenge the law affords. Third, it renders the decision amenable to meaningful judicial review, since a court cannot scrutinize the legality, rationality, or proportionality of a decision whose reasons are not disclosed. A decision without reasons is, for the purposes of judicial review, a decision without accountability. In the present cases, the impugned recommendations were effected without any speaking order articulating the basis of the Board’s adverse conclusions. No reasons were communicated to the petitioners. No material impugning their integrity was disclosed to them. The minutes of the Board’s meetings, to the extent available on the record, contain no express reference to the specific material that led the Board to entertain doubts regarding the petitioner’s fitness. This constitutes not merely a breach of natural justice but a blatant disregard of the express statutory mandate of section 24-A of the General Clauses Act, 1897. The discretion entrusted to the Board was exercised in a manner that is the precise antithesis of what the law requires i.e. in a manner without reasons, without disclosure, and without any demonstrated application of mind to the individual circumstances of each officer. On this ground alone, this Court is inclined to hold that the petitioner’s consideration for promotion was not meaningful and fair due to the failure to effectively communicate reasons, which as stated above is meant to ensure fairness and transparency.

We hope and trust that the appellant shall be given a proper assignment commensurate to his position in the service and the State Government in its action would exhibit no bias or mala fides. We make it clear that we have not examined the correctness of such allegations as we are sure given an opportunity the State Government would exhibit ideal conduct as an employer and establish by its conduct that the allegations were baseless.” Similarly, in the case of Syed Mehmood Akhter Naqvi and others vs. Federation of Pakistan and others, (PLD 2013 SC 195) the Honorable Supreme Court held:- “22. The principles of law enunciated hereinabove can be summarized as under:-- (i) … (ii) … (iii) … (iv) OSD: Officers should not be posted as OSD except for compelling reasons, which must be recorded in writing and are judicially reviewable. If at all an officer is to be posted as OSD, such posting should be for the minimum period possible and if there is a disciplinary inquiry going on against him, such inquiry must be completed at the earliest”

73. The Honorable Supreme Court of Pakistan in Corruption in Hajj Arrangements (Supra) Case examined the concept of OSD in considerable detail and unequivocally held that placing an officer as OSD is tantamount to penalizing W.P. NO’S. 989, 967, 1144, 2522, 1085, 1848 AND 1160 OF 2025 59 him because the expression itself is not known to civil servants laws of Pakistan and penalizing an officer through such administrative maneuver not only undermines the rule of law but also discourages honest officers who faithfully perform their duties in accordance with the Constitution and the law, and such actions may amount to a violation of Articles 3 of the Constitution. The superior courts have consistently deprecated the practice of keeping civil servants idle by designating them as OSDs for long periods, and such arrangements at best may be tolerated for a very brief transitional period where an officer is awaiting posting orders, but it cannot be allowed to continue for a prolonged duration. The that officers should not be kept as OSD for indefinite period and their services must be utilized in the public interest instead of allowing them to remain idle while drawing salary from the public exchequer. Another important safeguard emphasized by the superior courts is that even where exceptional circumstances justify a temporary OSD arrangement, the reasons for such action must be recorded in writing and must be capable of judicial scrutiny.

74. When the principles emerging from the above precedents are applied to the facts of the present case, the illegality of the impugned action becomes manifest. The OSD Notification does not disclose any reasons for placing the petitioner as OSD. The respondents have not asserted that any disciplinary proceedings or investigation are pending against the petitioner. He has remained in the said position for more than two years, which is far beyond the limited transitional period recognized by the courts. The petitioner is a senior officer of BPS-21 and his continued placement without duties not only undermines his professional dignity but also deprives the State of the services of a highly experienced officer. Such action therefore bears all the characteristics of an administrative penalty imposed without following the procedure prescribed by law. Administrative discretion, though wide, cannot be exercised arbitrarily or for extraneous purposes. The exercise of executive power must conform to the requirements of fairness, reasonableness and legality. Where the authority acts without recording reasons or in disregard of settled legal principles, such action becomes amenable to correction in constitutional jurisdiction. The continued placement of the petitioner as OSD, in the absence of compelling reasons and for an indefinite period, therefore constitutes an arbitrary exercise of power and cannot be sustained in law.

W.P. NO’S. 989, 967, 1144, 2522, 1085, 1848 AND 1160 OF 2025 60 75. In view of the above discussion, this Court finds the following:i. The 2017 Amendment was promulgated by the Prime Minister who framed and amended the Rules of 2010 in lawful exercise of authority personally delegated to him by the President under S.R.O. 120(I)/98 made under Section 25(1) of the Civil Servants Act, 1973. The principle in Mustafa Impex is inapplicable where the President has made an express and specific delegation directly to the Prime Minister; in that configuration the Prime Minister does not act as a surrogate for the Federal Government but as the President's authorised delegate. The expansion of the consultee class in the Note to Rule 5 falls within the broad latitude of the rule-making power and attracts no express or implied statutory prohibition. The 2017 Amendment is declared intra vires.

ii. The Impugned Notification (S.R.O. 35(I)/2025) whereby invitation was extended to Bilawal Bhutto Zardari and Khawaja Muhammad Asif was issued in exercise of sub-rule (1-A) inserted by S.R.O. 08(I)/2023 (which stands unchallenged), which expressly permits the Chairman to invite up to two Parliamentarians or Federal Ministers for consultation. The Impugned Notification is declared intra vires.

iii. The Chairman Amendment (S.R.O. 243(I)/2025) pursuant to which the Prime Minister exercised his own delegated rule-making power to restructure an executive function i.e. the chairmanship of the HPSB is not a sub-delegation of legislative authority and does not offend the principle of delegatus non potest delegare. The argument that the 29 th meeting was presided over by the Deputy Prime Minister rather than a Federal Minister is misconceived since Muhammad Ishaq Dar concurrently holds the office of Federal Minister for Foreign Affairs and is therefore a Federal Minister within the meaning of the amended rule, independently of his additional designation as Deputy Prime Minister. The Chairman Amendment is declared intra vires.

iv. The Reconsideration Amendment (S.R.O. 255(I)/2025) in which clause (v) inserted into Rule 4 of the Rules of 2010 imposes permanent ineligibility upon an officer considered twice without recommendation, regardless of the reasons for non-recommendation, whether those reasons W.P. NO’S. 989, 967, 1144, 2522, 1085, 1848 AND 1160 OF 2025 61 were ever communicated, and whether the earlier proceedings were themselves lawfully conducted. This provision bears no rational nexus to the merit-based purpose of Section 9 of the Act. It substitutes a procedural count for a substantive merit assessment, travels beyond the permissible limits of delegated legislation. The Reconsideration Amendment is declared ultra vires and is struck down.

v. On the question of meaningful consideration this Court finds that the recommendations of the HPSB are vitiated on three independent grounds. On illegality, the HPSB’s resolution to evaluate officers on attributes “as known to the Board members” confers an unbounded and unreviewable discretion untethered to the service record, which is impermissible. The criterion directing that recommendations of Departmental Representatives be given “due weightage” as “valuable inputs about the performance, integrity, and reputation of officers” is illegal and ultra vires the Rules of 2010, since the Departmental Representative is not a member of the HPSB and has no evaluative role, and a decision that is the result of another’s assessment is void for want of genuine statutory exercise. The minutes of the 29 th Meeting are completely silent on any evaluation of the petitioners’ experience, which is a mandatory statutory criterion under Rule 4(iv) of the Rules of 2010 and such silence is not a mere gap in articulation but is indicative of non-exercise of the Board’s power, and a decision reached without application of mind to a prescribed criterion is a decision made in in abdication of the jurisdiction conferred. On irrationality, in the cases of M. Aamir Zulfiqar Khan (W.P. No. 1160/2025) and Owais Nauman Kundi (W.P. No. 1848/2025), the Board acknowledged acceptable PERs and TERs while simultaneously awarding low grading which is an irreconcilable contradiction left unacknowledged and unexplained. In the cases of Sohail Ali Khan, Murtaza Khan, and Ms. Amna Imran, adverse integrity findings were recorded without reference to any entry or material in the service dossier, contrary to the maxim nemo fit repente turpissimus which fails the test of rationality and renders the recommendations unreasonable as under the Wednesbury unreasonableness. On procedural impropriety, the adverse material was never disclosed to the petitioners and no opportunity to respond was afforded, in violation of audi alteram W.P. NO’S. 989, 967, 1144, 2522, 1085, 1848 AND 1160 OF 2025 62 partem; and the petitioners were not recommended without communication of reasons, in breach of Articles 4, 10-A, and 19-A of the Constitution and Section 24-A of the General Clauses Act, 1897. A decision without reasons negates genuine application of mind, deprives the officer of any meaningful right of challenge, and forecloses judicial review. The recommendations of the HPSB given in its 29 th meeting (05– 10.03.2025), insofar as they pertain to the seven petitioners, are set-aside on the grounds of illegality, irrationality, and procedural impropriety. vi. The OSD Notification dated 25.01.2023, and the continued placement of the petitioner in W.P. No. 1160 of 2025 as an Officer on Special Duty beyond any reasonable transitional period, is unlawful, arbitrary, and is set-aside.

76. The cases of the petitioners for promotion shall be considered afresh with effect from the date of the Impugned Decisions, strictly in accordance with the law and the following directions:i. The HPSB shall confine itself to material in the official service dossier. It shall not rely upon personal knowledge, oral impressions, or unverifiable views of its member and the Departmental Representatives.
ii. Any adverse integrity finding shall be supported by specific reference to documentary material in the dossier. No such finding shall rest upon reputation, impression, or hearsay.
iii. In the event of non-recommendation, the Board shall record clear and specific reasons referable to each prescribed evaluation parameter or criteria.

iv. The reasons and material forming the basis of any adverse finding shall be communicated to the concerned officer within fourteen days of the conclusion of the fresh proceedings. Confidentiality shall not be invoked to deny the petitioners any minutes of meetings or reasons as the same pertains to and affects their rights.
v. The petitioner in W.P. No. 1085/2025 shall be considered for proforma promotion.
